title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers actually use and revise large language model (LLM)-generated formative feedback before sending it to students. Rather than comparing AI feedback against teacher or peer feedback in a controlled student-outcome experiment, the study focuses on a human-in-the-loop question: when an LLM drafts feedback on student short open-ended responses, how often do teachers accept, edit, or substantially change that feedback, and what kinds of changes do they make? The authors also test whether revision decisions can be predicted from the AI-generated text and analyze how revisions alter the pedagogical type of feedback.

The intervention context is the Tutoria platform, integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom, where an LLM generates an initial feedback draft for a student response and the teacher can accept it, edit it, or rewrite it before delivery. The dataset contains 1,349 AI-generated feedback instances and corresponding final teacher-delivered messages from 117 teachers. The data come from pooled prior controlled studies and classroom deployments across multiple contexts, including Brazilian high school chemistry classes and higher-education computer science settings. The LLMs used across development phases included GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) and later DeepSeek-V3 configurations. Quantitative analyses examine text length, semantic similarity, and prediction of revision behavior; qualitative coding classifies feedback into corrective, high-information, reinforcement/punishment, or other categories.

The main findings are that teachers accepted AI feedback unchanged in about 77.8% of cases, although revision behavior varied substantially across teachers. Edited feedback tended to start longer and was usually shortened by teachers while remaining semantically similar to the original, suggesting compression rather than wholesale correction. Predictive models using only AI text achieved modest above-chance performance for identifying which feedback would be revised (best AUC about 0.75). Qualitative coding showed that revisions often shifted feedback away from high-information explanatory forms toward shorter corrective forms. Overall, the paper concludes that default LLM feedback behavior is instructionally consequential because teachers often pass it through with little change, but when they do intervene, they tend to simplify and reframe feedback to better match their pedagogical priorities.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational/log-analysis study with descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and qualitative coding, but no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison on student outcomes. It provides useful real-world evidence on teacher use of AI feedback, yet causal credibility is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially meaningful operational benefits because most AI feedback was accepted without edits, but it does not estimate direct effects on student writing outcomes or teacher time saved in standardized effect-size terms. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback drafts for short open-ended student responses in the Tutoria platform, which teachers can accept, edit, or rewrite before sending to students.

finding.finding_summary: Across 1,349 AI-generated feedback instances handled by 117 teachers, teachers accepted AI feedback without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349), suggesting the system often reduced the need for manual rewriting. About 51.3% of teachers edited at least one message, but roughly half edited fewer than 6% of instances; edited messages were initially longer than unedited ones (48.3 vs. 41.9 words), and predictive models could identify likely revisions with fair accuracy (best AUC=0.75).
finding.measure: Teacher revision rate, proportion of accepted-as-is feedback, feedback word count, predictive accuracy of revision decisions (AUC, balanced accuracy, Cohen's kappa)
finding.effect_size: AUC=0.75; Cohen's w=0.16 for unrevised feedback type imbalance; Cramer's V=0.12 for shift after revision
finding.std_deviation: AI feedback length SD=19.60; final feedback length SD=19.81; edited AI feedback length SD=18.09; edited final feedback length SD=19.97

finding.finding_summary: The paper analyzed the pedagogical character of formative feedback on short open-ended responses in chemistry and computer science contexts, but it did not measure student learning gains. Qualitative coding of a deduplicated sample (N=834 messages) showed teacher revisions often shifted feedback away from high-information explanations toward more concise corrective forms, indicating changes in instructional style rather than demonstrated achievement effects.
finding.measure: Coded pedagogical feedback type (Corrective, High-information, Reinforcement/Punishment, Other) for AI-generated versus teacher-revised messages
finding.study_size: n=834 deduplicated feedback messages coded; source dataset n=1349 instances
